subject: Forensic Medicine
title: Post-Mortem Changes: Algor, Livor & Rigor Mortis
preview: Postmortem change is shaped by environment, body position and other variables; no single sign can determine an exact time of death.

sections.title: What the changes represent
points: Algor: the body generally equilibrates with its environment, at a variable rate.
Livor: dependent color change can indicate body position but is not a stand-alone clock.
Rigor: cross-bridge persistence develops with ATP depletion; onset and disappearance vary.

sections.title: Context matters
points: Decomposition, temperature, environment and postmortem handling can modify classic patterns.
An apparent fixed timeline in a textbook is only a crude teaching approximation, not an individual forensic estimate.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: A fixed degrees-per-hour cooling rule is not reliable for an unknown scene.
Do not assert that a single observation proves an exact time or manner of death.

quickRevision: Algor mortis is cooling after death and depends on temperature, clothing, body habitus and airflow.
Livor mortis reflects gravity-dependent pooling; rigor mortis reflects postmortem ATP depletion in muscle.
A reliable forensic interpretation combines scene evidence, several physical findings and the known history.

quiz.question: Why is one postmortem sign inadequate for exact time-of-death determination?
options: Environmental and biological factors alter its course
Rigor always follows a precise timetable
All bodies cool at one fixed universal rate
quiz.explanation: Environmental and biological factors alter its course. Do not assert that a single observation proves an exact time or manner of death.
